 Print Walking through an airport with a watch worth nearly Rs 1 crore on your wrist or tucked into your bag, is always a gamble if you skip the customs counter. One Indian passenger flying into New Delhi from Dubai found that out the hard way, ending up under arrest after customs officers intercepted him with a pre-owned Patek Philippe Aquanaut valued at Rs 94 lakh. The seizure at Indira Gandhi International (IGI) Airport has sparked the usual round of questions from frequent flyers: If you buy an expensive watch abroad, can you just wear it home? And does buying it second-hand get you off the hook for customs duty? How the interception played out at T3
 The stop happened on November 11 at Terminal 3 of IGI Airport. According to Delhi Customs (Airport and General), officers working off specific intelligence and passenger profiling flagged an Indian national who had just landed from Dubai on SpiceJet flight SG5106. Instead of letting him wave through the Green Channel, officers pulled him aside for X-ray screening and a thorough check of his bags and person. As he walked through the Door Frame Metal Detector (DFMD), the gate beeped. A closer search turned up the pre-owned Patek Philippe Aquanaut. Customs called in a Chartered Engineer to verify the piece, who confirmed it was authentic and pegged its value at Rs 94 lakh. Officers seized the watch under Section 110 of the Customs Act, 1962, and placed the flyer under arrest under Section 104. Sharing details of the bust on X on November 17, Delhi Customs used the case to remind international arrivals to declare dutiable items and head straight for the Red Channel instead of chancing the Green. Green channel vs. red channel: Where things went wrong
 Anyone who has walked out of international arrivals has seen the green and red signs, though plenty of travellers still treat them casually: Green Channel: Strictly for passengers carrying nothing that requires a customs declaration or duty payment. 
 Red Channel: For anyone bringing in restricted items, commercial quantities, or goods worth more than their duty-free limit.
 If an item you are bringing into India attracts customs duty, walking into the Green Channel is treated as a misdeclaration. In this case, officers were already watching out for the passenger based on intelligence inputs, and the investigation is still working through how he acquired the watch and why it wasn't declared. Does "pre-owned" mean duty-free?
 A common myth among international shoppers is that once you take the tags off a luxury watch or buy it pre-owned - customs treats it as an everyday personal belonging. Indian customs law doesn't work like that. Under India's Baggage Rules, 2026, eligible Indian residents and tourists of Indian origin flying into the country get a general duty-free allowance of Rs 75,000. While the rules do allow used personal effects needed for daily living during a trip to pass duty-free, a high-end Swiss timepiece worth nearly a crore rupees doesn't automatically qualify as an ordinary daily necessity just because it had a previous owner.  Whether an item passes without duty depends on what it is, when it was acquired, and whether the traveller actually declared it. Rs 94 lakh vs a rs 75,000 limit
 Put side by side, the numbers leave very little wiggle room. At Rs 94 lakh, the Patek Philippe Aquanaut was valued at more than 125 times the standard Rs 75,000 duty-free allowance for returning residents. Customs officials haven't released every detail of the passenger's statement yet, and the inquiry is still open. Still, the takeaway for anyone flying into India with high-value watches, jewellery, or luxury goods is straightforward: keep your paperwork handy, check the current baggage limits before you fly, and if you aren't sure whether something needs to be declared, walk through the Red Channel and ask. Paying duty at the counter is an inconvenience; getting arrested at the Green Channel is a far bigger problem.
